action_criteria.expected_evidence: Evans index 0.36 with DESH, callosal angle 72 degrees, temporal horn enlargement, patent aqueduct with flow void, Fazekas 2 without lacunes, MTA 1, no obstructing lesion
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with the iNPH markers: Evans index, callosal angle, temporal horns, DESH, aqueduct, periventricular signal and hippocampi
action_criteria.rationale: The outside report of enlarged ventricles needs measurement of the markers, grading of her white matter change and exclusion of an obstructing lesion.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Fasting glucose 108 mg/dL, HbA1c 6.4%; normal blood count, electrolytes, renal and thyroid function, B12 and folate; RPR and HIV non-reactive
action_criteria.label: Targeted labs for reversible contributors
action_criteria.rationale: Her diabetes and slowed thinking make a metabolic, thyroid and B12 screen good practice, but it does not decide iNPH.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 26 s with cane, 10-m walk 19 s in 29 steps, 180-degree turn in 8 steps, magnetic gait with freezing
action_criteria.label: Baseline timed gait assessment before the tap
action_criteria.rationale: Her TUG and 10-m walk must be timed before CSF is removed, with the cane she uses, so the post-tap change can be measured.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 23/30 with attention, executive and fluency deficits and relatively preserved recall
action_criteria.label: Bedside cognitive screen
action_criteria.rationale: A MoCA documents her slowed, frontal-subcortical profile against the outpatient MMSE of 25 and gives a baseline to repeat after the tap.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 13 cmH2O, normal cells, protein and glucose; 40 mL removed; TUG 26 to 17 s (35%) at 24 hours
action_criteria.label: CSF tap test: opening pressure, routine CSF and removal of 30-50 mL
action_criteria.rationale: Removing 40 mL with normal opening pressure and normal CSF content tests whether her gait improves when CSF is drained despite her white matter change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 21 s at 2 hours and 17 s at 24 hours (35% faster), 10-m walk 13 s (32% faster), MoCA 26/30
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating her cane-assisted TUG and 10-m walk at 2 and 24 hours after the 40 mL tap shows whether her gait responds to CSF removal despite the Fazekas 2 change.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]

Do not attribute the syndrome to small-vessel disease, or withhold shunt referral, on the basis of the Fazekas 2 white matter change when the ventricles are enlarged with DESH and the gait improves after the tap [Tisell_2011]
Do not attribute the gait difficulty to diabetes, deconditioning or age
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 35% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: She has had no seizures or fluctuating awareness, so an EEG does not address her progressive gait and cognitive syndrome.
Her near-falls happened while walking without loss of consciousness, so an ECG does not explain them.
She has no cardiac symptoms or embolic events, and an echocardiogram does not inform the iNPH work-up.
MRI is available and measures the callosal angle, DESH, white matter grade and hippocampi better than CT.
There is no syncope or palpitation history, so ambulatory rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
An 18-month course without rapid decline, fever or inflammatory features gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 white matter change in a hypertensive diabetic may contribute, but ventriculomegaly with DESH and a 35% TUG improvement after the tap are not explained by small-vessel disease.
Her mother had memory problems, but gait came first, recall is relatively preserved and cue-responsive, MTA is 1 and the MoCA rises after the tap.
Freezing overlaps, but there is no tremor, rigidity or orthostatic hypotension and the wide-based gait improves after the tap.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: A callosal angle of 72 degrees, DESH and ventricles disproportionate to the mild sulcal atrophy argue against ex-vacuo enlargement.

differential.diagnosis: Cervical or lumbar spondylotic myelopathy/radiculopathy contributing to gait
differential.key_features: Normal strength and tone, flexor plantars and intact joint position, with frontal release signs, urgency and cognitive slowing, point to a cerebral rather than a spinal cause.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH requires an insidious gait disturbance after age 40, progressing over at least 3 to 6 months without an antecedent cause, plus cognitive or urinary symptoms; she has all three over 18 months, gait first [Relkin_2005]
MRI shows Evans index 0.36 with both DESH components, a callosal angle of 72 degrees and temporal horn enlargement, with no obstructing lesion [Relkin_2005]
Opening pressure 13 cmH2O with normal CSF content meets the pressure criterion [Relkin_2005]

After removal of 40 mL, TUG fell from 26 to 17 s (35%) at 24 hours and the 10-m walk from 19 to 13 s; an improvement of 10% or more in TUG is a commonly used positive threshold, though no guideline sets a single cut-off
Fazekas 2 white matter change coexists with iNPH and does not preclude shunt benefit [Tisell_2011]
The tap test has a sensitivity of 26% to 61% and a PPV of 73% to 100%, so a clear response supports shunting while a negative tap would not have excluded it [Marmarou_2005]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-confluent Fazekas 2 change without lacunes does not account for ventriculomegaly with DESH or for a gait that improves 35% after CSF removal, and it does not preclude shunt benefit.
red_herrings.data_point: Periventricular and subcortical white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity (Fazekas grade 2) on brain MRI, with a prior CT 3 years ago noting 'minimal periventricular leukoaraiosis'
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent anchoring on white matter disease may attribute the gait and cognitive symptoms primarily to small-vessel vascular disease (VCI) and deprioritise the NPH workup, especially noting the history of hypertension and diabetes

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 3 required (brain MRI, baseline timed gait, CSF tap test), 1 recommended (post-tap gait reassessment) and 2 optional (labs, cognitive screen) actions; 1 grounded red herring; 5 differential alternatives.
metadata.difficulty_variant_description: iNPH in a 70-year-old woman with gait-predominant symptoms: Evans 0.36, callosal angle 72 degrees, DESH and a clear tap response (TUG 35% faster); Fazekas 2 white matter change in a patient with hypertension and diabetes is the red herring.
metadata.revision_reason: case-level re-audit of all NPH reviewer requests: the tap report is routed to CSF, timed gait/cognitive assessment is the required pre/post measure, the standalone neuropsychological battery and advanced imaging are removed from gold actions and callable authored follow-ups, laboratories remain optional, unrelated CSF assays are no longer returned for free, and the unsupported universal 20% response threshold is corrected

patient.chief_complaint: 18-month progressive difficulty walking, urinary urgency, and slowed thinking; referred for evaluation

family_history: Mother had memory problems in her 70s, unclear diagnosis
Father died of myocardial infarction at age 72
past_medical_history: Mild age-related white matter changes (noted on a CT 3 years ago, reported as 'minimal periventricular leukoaraiosis')

social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband; two adult children check in regularly

patient.history_present_illness: A 70-year-old right-handed retired schoolteacher with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin was admitted for evaluation of 18 months of progressive decline in gait, bladder control, and cognition. Her husband first noticed her gait change about 18 months ago: she began taking shorter steps, appeared to 'shuffle,' and her feet seemed to 'stick to the floor.' Over the next several months she had two near-falls and began using a cane. Gait symptoms are the most prominent and most distressing feature. Approximately 12 months ago she developed urinary urgency with occasional urge incontinence; she now wears a pad daily and has had nocturnal urgency waking her two to three times per week. Cognitive symptoms followed: her husband describes her as slower in conversation, repeating herself, and taking longer to manage finances and scheduling, tasks she previously performed effortlessly. She recalls her own cognition as 'slower, not forgetful.' MMSE obtained in the outpatient clinic was 25/30. A brain MRI ordered by her neurologist at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. A prior CT scan 3 years ago had noted only 'minimal periventricular leukoaraiosis.' Her neurologist referred her for progressive gait difficulty with slowed thinking and urinary urgency. She denies headache, diplopia, nausea, limb weakness, tremor, or sensory symptoms. No history of head trauma, meningitis, or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral frontal release signs: grasp reflex present bilaterally. No cogwheel rigidity. No orthostatic hypotension on standing (BP 134/82 lying, 130/80 standing).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-shin mildly clumsy bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements full, no nystagmus. No papilledema on fundoscopy. Facial sensation intact. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Magnetic, broad-based, short-stepped gait with markedly reduced foot clearance. Freezing at initiation and at doorway threshold. En bloc turning. Unable to tandem walk. Uses cane. Pull test: 2 steps backward, recovers without falling.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x4. Speech is fluent but mildly slowed. No aphasia. No perseveration. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone and strength throughout. No resting tremor. No cogwheel rigidity. No asterixis.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ biceps and brachioradialis bilaterally. 2+ patellar bilaterally. 1+ Achilles bilaterally. Bilateral plantar flexors.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration mildly reduced at ankles bilaterally (age-appropriate). Pinprick and light touch intact throughout. Joint position sense intact at toes.
